rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some say the seven dialects were allowed early to ease recitation, then readers converged on the final presentation when one reading became easy for them.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم: إن الترخيص في الأحرف السبعة كان في أول الإسلام لما في المحافظة على حرف واحد من المشقة عليهم أولا

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another view holds that readings outside the final presentation were abrogated.
rows.anchor: وبعضهم يقول إنه نسخ ما سوى ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Many scholars regarded readings attributed to Ubayy, Ibn Masud, and others that conflict with the codices as abrogated.
rows.anchor: ولذلك نص كثير من العلماء على أن الحروف التي وردت عن أبي وابن مسعود وغيرهما مما يخالف هذه المصاحف منسوخة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that Ibn Masud allowed reading by paraphrase is false; he said the readings are close and people should recite as they had been taught.
rows.anchor: نظرت القراءات فوجدتهم متقاربين فاقرءوا كما علمتم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Companions sometimes inserted or wrote explanatory tafsir alongside recitation because they knew what they had received from the Prophet and feared no confusion.
rows.anchor: كانوا ربما يدخلون التفسير في القراءة إيضاحا وبيانا لأنهم محققون لما تلقوه عن النبي

rows.speaker: مسروق
rows.claim: Masruq reports that Ibn Masud disliked tafsir being inserted into the Quran; another transmitter quotes him urging that the Quran be kept free of additions.
rows.anchor: فروى مسروق عنه أنه كان يكره التفسير في القرآن

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In a sound report through Zur ibn Hubaysh, Ibn Abbas says the Prophet presented the Quran to Gabriel annually and twice in his final year; Ibn Masud witnessed what was abrogated and changed, so his reading was the final one.
rows.anchor: قال لي ابن عباس أي القراءتين تقرأ؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Companions wrote what they verified as Quran and as un-abrogated, including soundly transmitted material not known to belong to the final presentation; this accounts for some codex differences.
rows.anchor: وإذ قد ثبت ذلك فلا إشكال أن الصحابة كتبوا في هذه المصاحف ما تحققوا أنه قرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the Companions had written only the final presentation, the codices would not differ through additions and omissions; they left aside what they had not verified.
rows.anchor: إذ لو كانت العرضة الأخيرة فقط لم تختلف المصاحف بزيادة ونقص وغير ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn al-Jazari describes this second Andalusian transmission chain for al-Dani's al-Taysir as sound and elevated, reaching the author through Andalusians.
rows.anchor: وهذا إسناد صحيح عال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Warsh was deaf but could hear Quran recitation; he read Nafi's reading repeatedly and wrote it down. Nafi once directed him to wait by a pillar for a reader.
rows.anchor: وكان أصم لا يسمع البوق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Warsh was born in 110 AH and died in Egypt in 197; after four complete readings with Nafi in Medina in 155, he returned to Egypt and became its leading recitation authority.
rows.anchor: وتوفي ورش بمصر سنة سبع وتسعين ومائة

rows.speaker: يونس بن عبد الأعلى
rows.claim: Yunus ibn Abd al-Ala praises Warsh's recitation, noting its clear hamza, lengthening, doubling, and grammatical articulation without tiring listeners.
rows.anchor: يونس بن عبد الأعلى كان ورش جيد القراءة حسن الصوت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Nishit died in 258 AH and was a trustworthy, precise, distinguished reciter; Ibn Abi Hatim called him truthful.
rows.anchor: وتوفي أبو نشيط سنة ثمان وخمسين ومائتين ووهم من قال غير ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Halwani died in 250 AH and was a major, reliable expert, especially in the Qalun and Hisham transmissions; he traveled to Qalun in Medina twice.
rows.anchor: وتوفي الحلواني سنة خمسين ومائتين وكان أستاذا كبيرا إماما في القراءات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Buwayan was born in 260 AH, died in 344, and was reliable and precise; Ibn Ghalbun's spelling of his name as Thuban is a corruption.
rows.anchor: وتوفي ابن بويان سنة أربع وأربعين وثلاثمائة ومولده سنة ستين ومائتين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qazzaz, whose death before 340 AH is given tentatively, was a trustworthy and highly exacting reciter.
rows.anchor: وتوفي القزاز فيما أحسب قبل الأربعين وثلاثمائة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn al-Ashath died shortly before 300 AH according to al-Dhahabi and was a reliable authority uniquely proficient in Qalun's reading from Abu Nishit.
rows.anchor: وتوفي ابن الأشعث قبيل الثلاثمائة فيما قال الذهبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Abi Mihran died in 289 AH and was a skilled, trustworthy reciter.
rows.anchor: وتوفي ابن أبي مهران سنة تسع وثمانين ومائتين وكان مقرئا ماهرا ثقة حاذقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jaafar ibn Muhammad died around 290 AH and was dependable in the Qalun transmission.
rows.anchor: وتوفي جعفر بن محمد في حدود التسعين ومائتين وكان قيما برواية قالون ضابطا لها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Azraq died around 240 AH, was reliable and precise, and succeeded Warsh in Egypt. He read with Warsh for a long time, completing twenty recitations in both rapid and measured styles; al-Khuzai says Egypt and the Maghrib knew no Warsh route but his.
rows.anchor: وتوفي الأزرق في حدود سنة أربعين ومائتين وكان محققا ثقة ذا ضبط وإتقان

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some performance scholars said Shuayb and Abu Hamdun only heard individual reading variants from Yahya ibn Adam, rather than presenting the Quran to him.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم: إنما قرآ عليه الحروف فقط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn al-Jazari says Shuayb heard the variants, whereas Abu Hamdun presented the Quran to Yahya ibn Adam; this is his preferred account over the claim that both only heard variants.
rows.anchor: والصحيح أن شعيبا سمع منه الحروف

rows.speaker: كثير من أهل الأداء
rows.claim: Many performance scholars say al-Ulaymi and Yahya ibn Adam both presented the Quran to Abu Bakr Shuba; another view says they only heard variants.
rows.anchor: وعرضا فيما أطلقه كثير من أهل الأداء على أبي بكر شعبة بن عياش

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some authorities deny that al-Ulaymi and Yahya ibn Adam presented the Quran to Shuba and say they only heard variants from him.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم: إنهما لم يعرضا عليه القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn al-Jazari distinguishes the transmissions: Yahya ibn Adam heard the variants from Shuba, while al-Ulaymi presented the Quran to him.
rows.anchor: والصحيح أن يحيى بن آدم روى عنه الحروف سماعا

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو الداني
rows.claim: Al-Dani says Ibn Mujahid recognized only al-Asha as having recited the full Quran to Abu Bakr, but asserts five others also did, naming four in this excerpt.
rows.anchor: قال الحافظ أبو عمرو الداني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In spellings such as mayah, mayatayn, malayh, and malayhim, the alif before yāʾ is additional and the yāʾ represents the hamza.
rows.anchor: فالألف في ذلك زائدة كما قدمنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn al-Jazari rejects al-Dani, al-Shatibi, and their followers' claim that the yāʾ in malayh and malayhim is additional: it is the hamza's written form.
rows.anchor: من الداني والشاطبي ومن قلدهما كيف قطعوا بزيادة الياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some initial hamzas are written according to how they are eased in connected speech, applying the medial spelling pattern to indicate that easing combines two Arabic pronunciations.
rows.anchor: بل صورت بحسب ما تخفف به حالة وصلها بما قبلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The dammated hamza in unabbikum is represented by waw after alif; comparable paired hamzas in other words are written with one alif to combine both written forms.
rows.anchor: فرسمت المضمومة في (أونبيكم) بالواو بعد الألف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same conventions cover paired and triple hamzas and selected initial-hamza forms written with yāʾ to represent connected pronunciation.
rows.anchor: وكذلك ما اجتمع فيه ثلاث ألفات لفظا نحو أآلهتنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hāʾulāʾ is written with waw and joined to the alerting particle with its alif omitted, as in yā ayyuhā.
rows.anchor: ثم وصل بها التنبيه بحذف ألفه كما فعل في (يأيها)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the Taha spelling yābna umm, the waw joins the word and the following alif belongs to ibn, not to the vocative particle, whose alif is omitted.
rows.anchor: فالألف التي بعد الياء هي ألف (ابن)

rows.speaker: أبو الحسن السخاوي
rows.claim: Al-Sakhawi identified the Damascus codex as evidence for the yābna umm spelling, and Ibn al-Jazari says he saw the same reading there, though the manuscript showed a mark of erasure.
rows.anchor: نص عليه أبو الحسن السخاوي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Sham codex cited by al-Sakhawi is kept at the northeastern Mashhad Ali in Damascus's Umayyad Mosque; trusted teachers said it had earlier been in the al-Kushk mosque in Damascus.
rows.anchor: بالمشهد الشرقي الشمالي الذي يقال له مشهد علي بالجامع الأموي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hamza reads the word for mercy with genitive inflection; the other readers use the nominative.
rows.anchor: فقرأ حمزة بالخفض، وقرأ الباقون بالرفع

words: إن نعف عن طائفة منكم نعذب طائفة
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asim reads both verbs with first-person nūn, fatha on نعف, kasra on the ذال of نعذب, and طائفة in the accusative; the others use third-person ya for the first verb, second-person ta for the second, and nominative طائفة.
rows.anchor: فقرأ عاصم نعف بنون مفتوحة وضم الفاء نعذب بالنون وكسر الذال طائفة بالنصب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yaqub lightens the ذال in المعذرون; the other readers double it.
rows.anchor: فقرأ يعقوب بتخفيف الذال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr use a damma on the sīn in دائرة السوء at both locations; the others use fatha, with Warsh following his usual lengthening of waw.
rows.anchor: فقرأ ابن كثير وأبو عمرو بضم السين في الموضعين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readers agree on fatha in these forms because سوء means evil as a verbal noun used emphatically as an adjective, like calling someone a man of truth or a man of evil.
rows.anchor: وصف به للمبالغة كما تقول هو رجل سوء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readers agree on damma in these occurrences because سوء means harm, misfortune, or affliction; where either sense fits, readings differ.
rows.anchor: لأن المراد به المكروه والبلاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yaqub reads the راء in والأنصار with nominative inflection; the other readers use the genitive.
rows.anchor: فقرأ يعقوب برفع الراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir adds من and reads تحتها with the source's lowered tāʾ; this matches Meccan codices, while other readers omit من and match their codices.
rows.anchor: فقرأ ابن كثير بزيادة كلمة " من "

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author suggests the omitted من distinguishes water springing from beneath the gardens' trees from water arriving from elsewhere and then flowing beneath them; the gardens are prepared for the named people as an honor.
rows.anchor: ينبع الماء من تحت أشجارها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hamza, al-Kisai, and Khalaf read نأكل with first-person plural nūn; the other readers read يأكل with third-person ya.
rows.anchor: فقرأ حمزة والكسائي وخلف بالنون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir, Ibn Amir, and Abu Bakr read the lām of ويجعل with nominative ending; the other readers use the jussive.
rows.anchor: فقرأ ابن كثير وابن عامر وأبو بكر برفع اللام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Jafar, Ibn Kathir, Yaqub, and Hafs read يحشرهم with ya; the remaining readers use nūn.
rows.anchor: فقرأ أبو جعفر وابن كثير ويعقوب وحفص بالياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Amir reads فيقول with nūn, while the other readers use ya.
rows.anchor: فقرأ ابن عامر بالنون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Jafar reads تتخذ passively with a dammated nūn and fatha on خ; the other readers use the active form with fatha on nūn and kasra on خ.
rows.anchor: فقرأ أبو جعفر بضم النون وفتح الخاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For Abu Jafar's passive reading, one analysis treats the pronoun in تتخذ as the passive subject and من أولياء as a second object; Ibn Jinni and others offer the better analysis: من أولياء is a circumstantial phrase with زائد من under negation, meaning they have no right to worship or claim allegiance to anyone besides God.
rows.anchor: وغيره أن يكون من أولياء حالا

rows.speaker: ابن شنبوذ
rows.claim: Ibn Shanabudh transmits Qunbul's third-person reading, also read by Ibn Haywa; Ibn Mujahid reports that Qunbul used the direct address, as do the remaining readers.
rows.anchor: فروى عنه ابن شنبوذ بالغيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hafs reads فما تستطيعون as direct address; the other readers use the third person.
rows.anchor: فروى حفص بالخطاب، وقرأ الباقون بالغيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Amr and the Kufan readers lighten the ش in تشقق at both locations; the others double it.
rows.anchor: فقرأ أبو عمرو، والكوفيون بتخفيف الشين فيهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir reads two nūns, with a light zāy, nominative verb, and accusative الملائكة, matching the Meccan codex; others use one nūn, doubled zāy, and nominative الملائكة.
rows.anchor: فقرأ ابن كثير بنونين الأولى مضمومة والثانية ساكنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two Medinan readers lighten the nūn; Ibn Amir's agreed reading has two light nūns, first fatha and second kasra, as in the Sham codex. Other transmitters of Ibn Dhakwan vary between one light nūn, two light nūns, or a choice of forms; the remaining readers use one doubled nūn.
rows.anchor: فقرأ المدنيان بتخفيف النون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Kufan readers lighten the ت in both occurrences of فتحت in this sura and at the location in al-Naba; the other readers double it.
rows.anchor: فقرأ الكوفيون بالتخفيف في الثلاثة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Medinan readers, Ibn Kathir, and Abu Amr open the speaker's additive yāʾ in إني أخاف.
rows.anchor: إني أخاف فتحها المدنيان، وابن كثير وأبو عمرو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Medinan readers open the additive yāʾ in إني أمرت.
rows.anchor: إني أمرت فتحها المدنيان إن أرادني الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hamza leaves the additive yāʾ in إن أرادني الله quiescent.
rows.anchor: إن أرادني الله أسكنها حمزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Medinan readers, Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr, and Asim open the additive yāʾ in يا عبادي الذين أسرفوا.
rows.anchor: ياعبادي الذين أسرفوا فتحها المدنيان، وابن كثير وأبو عمرو وعاصم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Medinan readers and Ibn Kathir open the additive yāʾ in تأمروني أعبد.
rows.anchor: تأمروني أعبد فتحها المدنيان، وابن كثير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yaqub's transmitter Rawh retains the yāʾ in يا عباد, with disagreement about whether it is retained at both states; Rawh also retains the yāʾ in فاتقون.
rows.anchor: ياعباد فاتقون أثبت الياء فيها رويس في الحالين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Susi retains the yāʾ in فبشر عبادي when joining, with disagreement about stopping; Yaqub follows his usual rule at pause.
rows.anchor: فبشر عبادي أثبتها وصلا مفتوحة السوسي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two Medinan readers, Hamza, al-Kisai, and Khalaf read the hamza in أن كنتم with kasra; the other readers use fatha.
rows.anchor: فقرأ المدنيان، وحمزة والكسائي وخلف بكسر الهمزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hamza, al-Kisai, Khalaf, and Hafs use a dammated ya, fatha on nūn, and doubled ش; the others use fatha on ya, quiescent nūn, and a light ش.
rows.anchor: فقرأ حمزة والكسائي وخلف وحفص بضم الياء وفتح النون وتشديد الشين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Medinan readers, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Amir, and Yaqub read عند الرحمن as an adverb; the others read عباد الرحمن as the plural of عبد.
rows.anchor: وابن كثير وابن عامر ويعقوب (عند) بالنون ساكنة وفتح الدال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two Medinan readers use two hamzas in أأشهدوا, the second eased, with a quiescent ش; Abu Jafar and Qalun insert an alif between them according to their established rule. Other readers use one hamza and a fatha on ش.
rows.anchor: فقرأه المدنيان (أأشهدوا) بهمزتين الأولى مفتوحة والثانية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Amir and Hafs read قال as a statement; the other readers use the imperative قل.
rows.anchor: فقرأ ابن عامر وحفص قال على الخبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Jafar reads جئناكم in the plural with nūn and alif; the other readers use the singular form with ta.
rows.anchor: فقرأ أبو جعفر (جئناكم) بنون وألف على الجمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr, and Abu Jafar read سقفا with fatha on sīn and a quiescent qāf; the others use a damma on sīn.
rows.anchor: فقرأ ابن كثير وأبو عمرو وأبو جعفر بفتح السين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yaqub reads نقيض with ya. Abu Bakr's transmitters differ: al-Ulaymi and several named routes through Yahya report ya, while Yahya's other routes and the remaining transmitters use nūn.
rows.anchor: فقرأ يعقوب بالياء، واختلف عن أبي بكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Medinan readers, Ibn Amir, and Yaqub read لينذر with direct address; al-Bazzi's transmitters differ, and the remaining readers use the third person. Al-Dani's unqualified attribution of the disagreement in al-Taysir does not fit his two routes.
rows.anchor: فقرأ المدنيان، وابن عامر ويعقوب بالخطاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Kufan readers add a hamza before الحاء and read إحسانا; other readers read حسنا without the hamza or alif, matching their respective codices.
rows.anchor: فقرأ الكوفيون إحسانا بزيادة همزة مكسورة قبل الحاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yaqub reads وفصله with fatha on ف and no alif; the other readers read وفصاله with kasra on ف and an alif after ص.
rows.anchor: فقرأ يعقوب وفصله بفتح الفاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hamza, al-Kisai, Khalaf, and Hafs read both verbs with first-person nūn and أحسن in the accusative; the others use a passive third-person form with أحسن nominative.
rows.anchor: فقرأ حمزة والكسائي وخلف وحفص بنون مفتوحة فيهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir, the two Basran readers, and Asim read وليوفيهم with ya; the remaining readers use nūn. Hisham's transmitters differ.
rows.anchor: فقرأ ابن كثير، والبصريان، وعاصم بالياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yaqub, Hamza, Asim, and Khalaf read يرى with a third-person ya and nominative مساكنهم; the others use direct-address ta and accusative مساكنهم.
rows.anchor: فقرأ يعقوب وحمزة وعاصم وخلف، يرى بياء مضمومة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Bazzi and al-Azraq open the additive yāʾ in أوزعني أن.
rows.anchor: أوزعني أن فتحها البزي والأزرق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Medinan readers, Ibn Kathir, and Abu Amr open the additive yāʾ in إني أخاف.
rows.anchor: إني أخاف فتحها المدنيان، وابن كثير وأبو عمرو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Medinan readers, Abu Amr, and al-Bazzi open the additive yāʾ in ولكني أراكم.
rows.anchor: ولكني أراكم فتحها المدنيان، وأبو عمرو والبزي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Medinan readers and Ibn Kathir open the additive yāʾ in أتعدانني أن.
rows.anchor: أتعدانني أن فتحها المدنيان، وابن كثير
